name: Connecticut

events.title: Ratified the Constitution
events.text: Connecticut ratified the Constitution on January 9, 1788, the 5th state to do so. The Constitution gave it 5 seats in the House until the first census.

events.title: Statewide (general ticket) elections
events.text: In the 1st through 24th Congresses (1789–1837), Connecticut elected all of its representatives statewide on a general ticket instead of by district.

events.title: 1790 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1790 census, Connecticut's House delegation grew from 5 to 7 seats.

events.title: 1800 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1800 census, Connecticut kept 7 seats in the House.

events.title: 1810 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1810 census, Connecticut kept 7 seats in the House.

events.title: 1820 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1820 census, Connecticut's House delegation shrank from 7 to 6 seats.

events.title: 1830 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1830 census, Connecticut kept 6 seats in the House.

events.title: 1840 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1840 census, Connecticut's House delegation shrank from 6 to 4 seats.

events.title: 1850 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1850 census, Connecticut kept 4 seats in the House.

events.title: 1860 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1860 census, Connecticut kept 4 seats in the House.

events.title: 1870 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1870 census, Connecticut kept 4 seats in the House.

events.title: 1880 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1880 census, Connecticut kept 4 seats in the House.

events.title: 1890 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1890 census, Connecticut kept 4 seats in the House.

events.title: 1900 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1900 census, Connecticut's House delegation grew from 4 to 5 seats.

events.title: Some members elected at-large
events.text: In the 58th through 62nd Congresses (1903–1913), Connecticut elected one of its representatives statewide (at-large) and the rest by district.

events.title: 1910 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1910 census, Connecticut kept 5 seats in the House.

events.title: 1930 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1930 census, Connecticut's House delegation grew from 5 to 6 seats.

events.title: Some members elected at-large
events.text: In the 73rd through 88th Congresses (1933–1965), Connecticut elected one of its representatives statewide (at-large) and the rest by district.

events.title: 1940 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1940 census, Connecticut kept 6 seats in the House.

events.title: 1950 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1950 census, Connecticut kept 6 seats in the House.

events.title: 1960 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1960 census, Connecticut kept 6 seats in the House.

events.title: 1970 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1970 census, Connecticut kept 6 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: Donnelly v. Meskill
events.text: After the governor vetoed the legislature's congressional plan and all parties agreed the 1964 districts no longer met population standards, a federal court chose a plan based on the vetoed bill, with a 0.4% population deviation.

events.title: 1980 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1980 census, Connecticut kept 6 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 1990 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1990 census, Connecticut kept 6 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: Commission redraws map for five seats
events.text: With Connecticut dropping from six seats to five, the backup Reapportionment Commission missed its first deadline. The state Supreme Court gave it until December 21, 2001, and the commission adopted a congressional plan that day by a 9–0 vote.

events.title: 2000 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2000 census, Connecticut's House delegation shrank from 6 to 5 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 2010 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2010 census, Connecticut kept 5 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: Court adopts special master's map
events.text: When neither the legislature nor the backup commission agreed on a congressional plan, the Connecticut Supreme Court had a special master draw one and adopted it on February 10, 2012.

events.title: 2020 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2020 census, Connecticut kept 5 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: Court adopts congressional map
events.text: After the state's bipartisan redistricting commission missed its deadline, the Connecticut Supreme Court adopted a congressional map drawn by a special master in February 2022.

compactnessNote: Polsby-Popper compactness (4π × area ÷ perimeter²) measured on the projected district shapes. It describes shape only: coastlines, rivers and county lines lower it too, so a low score is not evidence of intent. "Irregular" marks the least compact 5% of district shapes in each census era nationally.

c025.text: Connecticut's district lines were redrawn between censuses, first used in the 1836 election. The reason has not been researched yet.

c028.text: New map drawn after the 1840 census, which cut Connecticut's seats from 6 to 4. It was first used in the 1842 election.

c063.text: New map drawn after the 1910 census, which left Connecticut with 5 seats. It was first used in the 1912 election.

c073.text: After the 1930 census raised Connecticut's seats from 5 to 6, the state kept its existing districts and elected one member statewide (at-large).

c089.text: New map drawn after the 1960 census, which left Connecticut with 6 seats. It was first used in the 1964 election.

c093.text: New map following: Donnelly v. Meskill. After the governor vetoed the legislature's congressional plan and all parties agreed the 1964 districts no longer met population standards, a federal court chose a plan based on the vetoed bill, with a 0.4% population deviation.

c098.text: New map drawn after the 1980 census, which left Connecticut with 6 seats. It was first used in the 1982 election.

c103.text: New map drawn after the 1990 census, which left Connecticut with 6 seats. It was first used in the 1992 election.

c108.text: New map following: Commission redraws map for five seats. With Connecticut dropping from six seats to five, the backup Reapportionment Commission missed its first deadline. The state Supreme Court gave it until December 21, 2001, and the commission adopted a congressional plan that day by a 9–0 vote.

c113.text: New map following: Court adopts special master's map. When neither the legislature nor the backup commission agreed on a congressional plan, the Connecticut Supreme Court had a special master draw one and adopted it on February 10, 2012.

c115.text: Not a new map: the historical boundary records show only slight differences in 3 districts from the previous Congress, and no statewide redistricting is recorded for this election.

c118.text: New map following: Court adopts congressional map. After the state's bipartisan redistricting commission missed its deadline, the Connecticut Supreme Court adopted a congressional map drawn by a special master in February 2022.
